title: Lab Cadence — Gradient Step-Flow Standup
description: A compact, Korean-leaning bilingual weekly-meeting slide built around a 1→2→3 step-flow layout of outlined summary cards and line-art icons — research-log practicality over conference-room ceremony.
philosophy: This template occupies the space between a Notion research-ops doc and a formal seminar deck: the Friday lab standup where everyone already knows the project and just needs to trace the week's experiment chain at a glance. It values scan speed and information density, rejecting decorative padding, heavy typographic hierarchy, and the ceremonial weight of paper-review slides. The lavender-to-cyan gradient numerals signal sequential progression without theatrics, and the Korean-first bilingual body type honors the internal audience rather than performing internationalization for outsiders. It belongs on shared lab monitors and small meeting-room screens, not auditorium projectors.
goodFor: Weekly lab standups summarizing 3–5 sequential experiment updates
Internal bilingual (Korean/English) status reviews among team members who share context
Step-by-step pipeline or methodology walkthroughs with single-line card summaries
Research-ops sprint check-ins replacing a shared Notion page
avoidFor: Public conference or academic paper presentations requiring formal visual polish
Chart-heavy quarterly data reviews with multi-axis visualizations
Executive briefings expecting high-ceremony layout and branded hierarchy
Audiences unfamiliar with lab-internal notation or iterative experiment framing
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide carries the quiet authority of a well-maintained lab notebook cover: purposeful and spare, not performative. Compositional weight is left-anchored with deliberate open space on the right interrupted only by a single gradient accent — a calm promise of the numbered flow ahead. Korean and English coexist as visual equals, neither language decorating the other. Avoid any ornamentation, hero imagery, or layered shadows that would tip the register from internal research document toward conference ceremony.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with the title block occupying cols 1–8, vertically anchored roughly one-fifth from the top edge; Korean title leads as the dominant text unit with the English subtitle directly beneath, divided by a single hairline rule. A gradient step-numeral or abstract gradient bar bleeds across the right quarter (cols 9–12) as a structural accent, implying the sequential flow of the deck without elaboration. No header band; a session date or edition label sits bottom-right at minimal scale. Side margins stay tight — roughly 6% — to reinforce the compact, lab-monitor-native character.

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like a well-maintained research log pinned to a shared lab monitor — functional urgency without ornamentation. Three equal-weight outlined cards form a horizontal step chain, each self-contained yet unmistakably part of an ordered sequence; the overall rhythm is dense-modular and scan-fast, never ceremonious. Line-art icons remain skeletal scaffolding for the eye rather than decorative focal points, always subordinate to the bilingual text lines. Avoid theatrical drop shadows, gradient washes behind card interiors, or any asymmetric visual drama that reads as conference-keynote rather than Friday standup.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with a slim header band (roughly the top 12% of the frame) holding the slide title and a paired bilingual section label; three equal-width outlined cards span the remaining height, distributed across the full column width with tight but consistent internal gutters. Each card contains a gradient step numeral anchored top-left, a skeletal line-art icon top-right, one primary Korean label line, and a compact English subtitle beneath it — all enclosed by a thin-stroke rectangular border with no fill. Hierarchy is established through size contrast between the step numeral and the body lines alone; no rule bands, background fills, or indentation layers are used inside the cards. Page number sits bottom-right flush to the outer margin; no footer band.
